Take with or after food to reduce GI upset

summary: Azathioprine is a thiopurine immunosuppressant (prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine) used to prevent renal transplant rejection and to treat rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune disease. It carries a boxed warning for increased risk of malignancy (lymphoma, including hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma) and causes dose-dependent myelosuppression; TPMT/NUDT15 status and CBC monitoring guide dosing.
indications: Adjunct for prevention of rejection in renal homotransplantation
Management of active rheumatoid arthritis to reduce signs and symptoms
Off-label: inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis), autoimmune hepatitis, systemic lupus, vasculitis, pemphigus and other autoimmune conditions

dosage.d: 3-5 mg/kg once daily starting at time of transplant
dosage.n: Begin on or 1-3 days before transplant
Do not raise to toxic levels for threatened rejection

dosage.d: ~1.0 mg/kg/day (50-100 mg) once daily or split BID
Increase by 0.5 mg/kg/day at 4-week intervals to max 2.5 mg/kg/day
Substantially reduce dose or avoid; homozygous deficient should not receive standard doses

admin: Take orally with or after food to reduce nausea
Handle as a hazardous/cytotoxic drug; avoid crushing tablets
Determine TPMT and NUDT15 status before or early in therapy where available
Therapeutic response in RA may take 6-12 weeks; do not discontinue prematurely
Reduce concomitant doses markedly when given with allopurinol/febuxostat
moa: Azathioprine is a prodrug that is non-enzymatically converted to 6-mercaptopurine, then to 6-thioguanine nucleotides which are incorporated into DNA and inhibit purine synthesis. This suppresses proliferation of lymphocytes (especially T cells), reducing cell-mediated and humoral immune responses. Activity depends on tissue thiopurine nucleotide levels rather than plasma drug concentration.

absolute: Use in rheumatoid arthritis during pregnancy
RA patients previously treated with alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, melphalan) due to prohibitive malignancy risk
relative: Pre-existing significant hepatic or renal impairment
monitor: Concurrent allopurinol or febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors)
Concurrent ACE inhibitors or co-trimethoprim (additive myelosuppression)

preg: Contraindicated in rheumatoid arthritis. In transplantation use only if the benefit outweighs the risk; it crosses the placenta and has been associated with low birth weight, prematurity and neonatal cytopenias. Advise effective contraception for both sexes during treatment.
lact: 6-mercaptopurine metabolites are detectable in breast milk. Breastfeeding is generally not recommended; if continued, monitor the infant for myelosuppression.
renal: Excretion is partly renal; reduce dose in renal impairment as accumulation of metabolites increases toxicity. Azathioprine and 6-MP are partially dialyzable.
hepatic: May cause hepatotoxicity including cholestasis and rare veno-occlusive disease. Use with caution and monitor LFTs; reduce dose or discontinue if liver injury develops.

major: Allopurinol / febuxostat - block xanthine oxidase causing markedly increased 6-MP and severe myelosuppression; reduce azathioprine dose to ~25-33% (avoid febuxostat)
Live attenuated vaccines - risk of disseminated infection in immunosuppressed patients
Other myelosuppressive/immunosuppressive agents - additive marrow toxicity and infection risk
moderate: ACE inhibitors - increased risk of anemia and leukopenia
Warfarin - azathioprine may reduce anticoagulant effect
Ribavirin - inhibits metabolite formation and worsens cytopenias
minor: Aminosalicylates (mesalamine, sulfasalazine) - may inhibit TPMT and increase thiopurine levels
interactions.food: May be taken with food to reduce GI upset; no major food interaction.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol due to additive hepatotoxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: Causes macrocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and elevated transaminases; monitor blood counts and LFTs.

rare: Malignancy - post-transplant lymphoma, skin cancers, hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma

monitoring: Complete blood count weekly during the first month, then 1-2 weekly to month 3, then monthly (more often after dose changes)
TPMT and NUDT15 genotype/phenotype before or early in therapy where available
Monitor for signs of infection and unusual lumps/skin lesions (malignancy surveillance)
counsel: Report fever, sore throat, unusual bruising or bleeding promptly (low blood counts)
Use sun protection and report new skin lesions (skin cancer risk)
Use effective contraception; do not breastfeed during therapy
Avoid live vaccines and inform all providers you are immunosuppressed
Tell your doctor before starting allopurinol or febuxostat
pk: Clinical immunosuppressive effect over weeks (RA 6-12 weeks)
Serum 6-MP/metabolite peak 1-2 hours after oral dose
Parent ~5 hours (35-S metabolites); effect outlasts plasma levels
Store 20-25 C in a dry place; protect from light
pearls: Boxed warning: chronic immunosuppression increases risk of malignancy including lymphoma (post-transplant lymphoma and hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma in IBD)
Check TPMT/NUDT15 before dosing - deficient patients risk life-threatening myelosuppression
With allopurinol/febuxostat, reduce azathioprine to about a quarter to a third of the usual dose (avoid febuxostat)
Therapeutic effect in autoimmune disease may take 6-12 weeks - do not stop early for lack of response
Counsel sun protection and regular skin checks due to non-melanoma skin cancer risk
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual schedule. Do not take a double dose.
overdose: Acute overdose causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea acutely, with delayed myelosuppression as the main risk. There is no specific antidote; azathioprine and 6-MP are partially dialyzable. Provide supportive care with frequent blood count monitoring; consider gastric decontamination if recent and treat infection/cytopenias.
